en: Ajybay and I were the strongest
Of the forty companions, and we were khans.
While noble Manas lived,
Even when only we two remained,
We were men like prophets!
Now my camp has shifted and the night has passed;
Alas, while Manas lived,
Those joyful days passed too.
The land remains, but he is gone;
When I reflect, such days have passed.
Leaving Khan Bakai to lament,
This cruel world has tormented me!”
Their uncle, elder Bakai,
His golden-cheeked battle-axe
Braced against his side, groaning,
Mighty Bakai in his ordo
Slumped down with a groan!
His former grief flared anew;
The breast of your mighty uncle Bakai
Rattled and heaved,
His beard trembling strand by strand;
Tears flowing from both eyes
Quivered down over his chest!
On this side lay the Kara-Suu,
With their ears pricked upright,
It was a land where wolves roamed;
With their tails trailing behind,
It was a land where foxes roamed.
Crawling over the sands by day,
Its young were as large as yearling colts,
Galloping proudly like young horses,
They played over the open plain!
Its wonders dazzled the eye;
No living man could tire of them.
Its cold allowed no mosquitoes!
In the fiercest forty days of winter,
Kites, falcons, and saker falcons—
These birds made the place their home.
It curved through hillock after hillock;
Deer poured out from the hummocks.
The trail descended toward the saddlebags,
Where the grass on the hummocks grew sparse.
Wild asses snorted on the level ground;
What a wondrous place this Jyldyz was—
Snakes hissed in the gullies!
Beyond Kichi-Jyldyz,
On this side of Chon-Jyldyz,
The projecting headland of Kara-Kyr—
The land Khan Almam made his home,
This is the sacred place!
At Kara-Kyr stand twin tombs,
Called the Chymam tombs;
The place where true elder Ala camped
Was a sacred place.
All around it the air whistled,
With wind blowing in a circle.
It was a homeland
Of the mighty heroes of old.
Its surroundings were secure;
They called it the Chymam tomb.
It had firewood and water;
For the boys left horseless and on foot,
It was a place to remain with the baggage train!
It had a ridge from which to keep watch.
The wary lion Bakai
Had seen it, the mighty one.
When he climbed to the lookout and gazed,
Seeking safe ground,
When he turned his face to the right,
The gray haze divided;
When he looked this way,
A dim desert appeared.
Your falcon, uncle Bakai,
Unwilling to remain in that place,
Then felt his heart torn!
He marked down the day, they say,
And reckoned the count of days.
He marked down the month,
And reckoned the count of months.
Clasping hands and speaking together,
Saying, “Farewell, remain safe!”
They made their promise firm.
His white beard gleaming,
Cackling like a migrating goose,
Speaking softly but firmly,
Their uncle Bakai began:
“Springs flowing through the valley,
My champions, precious as children seen late in life,
Unless what I tell you is false,
Unless my God himself knows otherwise,
That is the place called Chet-Beijing;
Those are the Chinese people with their army.
When their wrath is aroused,
They are a flood that overwhelms!
While my bloodthirsty lord lived,
I am lion Bakai, who fought them
For months and years!
Beyond the gray-hazed mountain neck,
That is the pass beyond Beijing.
With eyes reddened like a raven's,
My pale beard trailing,
Parted from my companions,
I am wretched Bakai!
While the lions lived,
This is where we shot the Alengir bow;
Against the teeming infidels,
Waging battle there,
This is where we seized their khanate!
This is where we slaughtered many of their people,
Plundered their daughters, and rested!
I know the road to Beijing well;
My valiant boys, wait without haste.
It is ill-fated that you were left on foot!
This is darkness, this is night;
If a brave man is parted from his horse,
This is the day of the end of time!
I have begun my journey to Beijing;
Champions left behind by the hero,
I have left you with the baggage train!
The outward journey is three months,
The return journey another three months;
Your noble uncle Bakai—
Look for him in the sixth month!
If I fail to return by the sixth month,
Shoot an argali and eat it,
And depart saying, ‘Our uncle,
Elder Bakai, has died.’
Cross through the water of that distant caravan route;
Lamenting in grief,
Saying, ‘Both our uncles died together,’
Give up hope of us and go!
The cannon the Creator ordained—
We go to see it;
If our doom comes from the khagan,
We go there to die!
To Beijing, where even a prophet would not tread,
To unleash a wondrous slaughter,
And in the khagan's Beijing
To avenge the mighty hero!”
So saying and exhorting them, the gray wolves
Rode out and took the road,
Leaving the boys with the baggage train.
Your champion, the bloodthirsty man's son,
Born especially
Of his father, noble Manas,
The lone hero, son of the gray wolf,
Mounted Buurul and made him surge,
The splendid hero rode out,
Making him leap and strain.
“I shall bind my belt tightly,” he said;
“I myself shall face them,
And from the Kalcha in Beijing
Seek vengeance for the valiant man.
I shall spend upon Beijing
All the strength gathered in my hands;
I ask the Creator
For the single faith within my breast!
The one I shall grapple is the khagan of China;
The one I oppose is Bakburchun.
I go to grapple with its khan,
Marching on a holy campaign
To Khan Kongurbai's city,
For my father, lion Manas,
For the hero gone to the next world!
Against that hero Kongurbai,
I go beginning a holy campaign,
Against the infidel full of wrath.”
Such was his word of counsel.
Leaving the boys with the baggage train,
They repaired and donned their ak-olpok armor;
They buckled around their waists
The gray cartridge pouch left by Manas.
The boys wailed and wept,
Entreating the Almighty!
His anguish smoking fiercely,
Külchoro stood sobbing;
Beside him was steadfast Kanchoro,
Known as the son of Chubak,
His dear eyes like a saker falcon's,
Unblinking, filled with tears,
The very heavens grieved though they had no horse:
“If only we could go
To Beijing, city of the Chinese khagan,
Against the Black Chinese and Manchus,
To stand as support for the bloodthirsty hero
And fight beside him;
Against the broad-booted, cotton-sashed,
Kongurbai, khan of the Kechil,
That swaggering swine,
To take revenge on him—
If only we could meet him;
Against the vengeful Kechil,
If only we could face him;
Against the Black Chinese and Manchu people,
If only we could encounter them;
Against the teeming Chinese,
To stand beside the gray wolf
And die together!
Without spare horses, we two
Are fated to remain at the pass;
Our grief is great, but there is no remedy—
We are fated to remain at the pass!”
Grieving, the boys said:
“Against Kaldai in his karapjy,
We did not charge and strike with spears;
Against the Manchu in his otogot,
We did not duel him with loud cries,
Nor stand wreaking havoc!
With no tulpars beneath us,
We did not go and see Beijing;
We did not support the gray wolf,
Face the enemy, and die!
With neither khans nor people,
We are fated to remain in the desert!
Parted from the noble heroes,
These glass-bright eyes shedding tears,
We are fated to remain at the pass!
If noble Bakai and Semetey
Return safely, our road is blessed;
If by chance Beijing defeats them,
Our sorrow will never heal!
When one longs for it, is there
A night like the sacred Night of Power?!
Will the day come when my khan and uncle
Returns after battle and plunder?
Will the day come when my warrior uncle
Returns without leaving us to grieve?!
If by chance the two khans perish,
We shall see every misery;
Unable to cross the ridge,
Unable to reach a known people,
We shall die while traveling on foot!
A thick net drawn before us,
Heavy misfortune fixed upon our brows!
Our tulpars were sent against the foe,
And our road became beset with hardship!
Go safely and return safely,
You two great men who sustain our hopes!”
Distraught, the boys said this;
Like children whose mother had gone,
Their spirits were torn,
Many thoughts returning to mind,
Tears pouring from their eyes!
They stood grieving bitterly,
Their lot dark with misery.
Sorrowing and mourning,
The boys remained on the plain,
Parted from the two lions.
The boys now remained with the baggage train;
Bakai now rode out to scout.
Along a winding road,
Beside the winding Kara-Suu,
Curving onward on the way,
Your uncle, lion Bakai,
Rode far without sparing his horse.
The perfect tulpar Kökcholok—
